tagline: Mountain towns and a former toll road lead toward Mount Mitchell.
intro: Mount Mitchell Scenic Drive links mountain towns, the South Toe River Valley and the Black Mountains. The North Carolina Department of Transportation presents the byway as a journey through mountain scenery, recreation and Appalachian culture. Its guide gives 52.5 miles and a driving time of one hour and 20 minutes. On NC 128, the two-lane summit road climbs in mild curves to a parking lot below the peak. The South Toe drains the eastern slopes of the Black Mountains; farms, pastures and small communities occupy the rural stretches of Yancey and Madison counties.

That summit approach predates the scenic designation: a 1936 county map shows it as a toll road. It received the number NC 128 on or around 1947. In 2011, the Mount Mitchell Scenic Drive designation joined it with the Blue Ridge Parkway, NC 80 and US 19 and 19E in a corridor reaching I-26.

Traveling toward the summit, start at I-26 Exit 9 and follow the corridor through Burnsville and Micaville. Burnsville brings a town square and quilt blocks on barns and businesses at the west end of town. Beyond Micaville, NC 80 follows the South Toe before reaching the Parkway at Buck Creek Gap. The Parkway and NC 128 complete the climb to the summit parking lot.

moments.title: Burnsville
moments.text: A naval officer gives this mountain town its name: Captain Otway Burns, a hero of the War of 1812. Burnsville was founded in 1834 on land conveyed by John "Yellow Jacket" Bailey. In 1909, Burns's grandson gave the town a statue, placed on a granite pedestal in the square. Damage led to replacement of the original statue in the early 2000s. At the west end of town, quilt blocks on barns and businesses belong to the Quilt Trails of Western North Carolina; their patterns reflect the heritage of each location.

moments.title: Micaville
moments.text: Micaville takes its name from the mica mined here. In the early 1900s, the Black Mountain Railroad helped change an agricultural economy into a mining economy, with lumber harvesting added later. The line later operated as the Yancey Railroad. Its freight included mica and feldspar as well as fertilizer, building materials, livestock feed and steel spring wire. Hurricane Agnes and flooding from other storms destroyed most of its bridges, track and branches. NCDOT directs travelers to look for traces of old mining operations in town. The area was known for the large sheets of mica extracted from its mines.

moments.title: Mount Mitchell
moments.text: The road ends below the summit; a steep paved trail continues through conifer forest to the top. Mount Mitchell reaches 6,684 feet, the highest peak east of the Mississippi in mainland North America. Elisha Mitchell explored the Black Mountains in 1835 and determined that the range exceeded Mount Washington in New Hampshire. Returning to verify his measurements in 1857, he fell to his death at Mitchell Falls. The summit observation deck opened in 2009, replacing a stone tower demolished in 2006. The summit trail measures 980 feet, continuing the journey beyond the parking lot on foot.

practical: Mount Mitchell: NCDOT prohibits tractor-trailers on the route and does not recommend it for recreational vehicles or buses. When weather closes the Blue Ridge Parkway, access to NC 128 is cut off. (checked 2026-10-11)
